Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Pillars: Not One Self · Unfinished Is Honest

The Questions

Mr. Spitzer is “many selves who had been none.” How can a multitude add up to no one?

He is like “a mystery which is completed and laid away… an empty shell.” Is the finished, solved self a fullness or a vacancy?

A tailor duns him for a suit already paid, a tailor who “perhaps… had never existed.” What is a debt owed to a phantom?

The paid bill keeps arriving. What account can never be closed?

The chapter states Not One Self in its most vertiginous form: Mr. Spitzer is “many selves who had been none.” The multitude does not add up to a rich fullness here but to a vacancy, a crowd that is also an absence, the many somehow summing to no one. This is the plurality pushed past celebration and past mere fraying into paradox: to be many can be to be none, the selves so numerous and so unintegrated that there is no one there at all, only the crowd and, at its center, nobody. The book has held the plural self as the ordinary truth; here it looks straight at the vertigo in that truth, the possibility that a self of many is a self of none.

And the chapter attaches the vacancy, tellingly, to the finished. Mr. Spitzer is “self-contained like a mystery which is completed and laid away, a psychic armor no one now investigates, an empty shell.” The completed mystery is the empty one. Once a thing is solved, sealed, laid away, no longer investigated, it is armor with no one inside, a shell. This is the book’s dread of the finished stated at the level of a person: to be a completed self, a solved and closed identity, would be to be an empty shell, and Mr. Spitzer’s refusal to cohere, his staying many and unsolved, is what keeps him from being that vacant finished thing. The empty shell is what a sealed self looks like.

The tailor’s bill is the chapter’s comic and exact image of the unclosable. A tailor keeps dunning Mr. Spitzer for a suit “he was quite certain he had already paid for,” a suit for the dead brother, and the tailor himself “perhaps had never existed.” So a phantom bills him for a settled debt, and the paid account will not stay paid. This is Unfinished Is Honest turned into farce: some accounts cannot be closed, some debts keep arriving after settlement, some matters refuse the final receipt. Mr. Spitzer has “no receipts, no cancelled checks,” nothing to prove the thing finished, because the thing cannot be finished, and the phantom tailor will go on dunning a debt that was paid and may never have been owed.

The three hold together. A self of many that is also none, a finished mystery that is an empty shell, and a paid debt that will not close are one recognition in three keys: that completion is vacancy and incompletion is life. What is solved is laid away empty; what stays open, the unclosable account, the uncohered self, the debt still arriving, is where the person actually is. Mr. Spitzer is kept from the empty shell precisely by his failure to be finished, and the tailor’s endless bill, absurd as it is, is the sound of a life refusing to be settled and filed.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes “many selves who had been none” for simple emptiness, a man reduced to nothing, and the reading that takes the phantom tailor’s bill for mere whimsy. Neither the reduction to nothing nor the whimsy is what the chapter shows.

The footing is that the plural self can sum to none, a crowd that is also a vacancy, and that this vertigo is the truth looked at squarely rather than a defect; that the finished, solved, laid-away self is the empty shell, so completion is vacancy and Mr. Spitzer’s refusal to cohere is what keeps him from being hollow; and that some accounts cannot be closed, the paid debt still arriving, the receipt never final, because incompletion is life. The solved self is empty and the open one is alive. The phantom tailor duns a settled debt forever, and the chapter lets the account stay open.

For Reflection

Can a self of many turn out to be a self of none, and is that emptiness or honesty?

Is the completed, solved, filed-away self a fullness, or an empty shell with no one inside?

What paid debt or settled matter in one’s life refuses, still, to close?

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Pillars: Not One Self · Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The Questions

Mr. Spitzer will not “disturb the dreamer.” Is that cowardice, cruelty, or the truest kindness the chapter knows?

Catherine says her “drugged vision provided more of reality than reality provided.” Inside a sealed world, is that a lie?

Who is Mr. Spitzer, when strangers take him for his dead brother and he half-agrees?

What is the black coachman that Catherine cannot stop hunting?

This is the chapter where Mr. Spitzer becomes the Witness. Catherine lives inside her sealed dream, and he could puncture it; he is a lawyer, made of logic, and her irrationality baffles him. But he holds back. He is unwilling “to rob her, to disturb the dreamer and the precarious dream.” He stays in the room with her sealed world and does not correct it, does not fix or wrap it up, and that staying is the stance the book most trusts, arriving here in the man who will carry it through the middle of the novel.

The stance is tender and it is not simple. To witness Catherine’s dream is not to endorse it; her invention is sealed, her “drugged vision provided more of reality than reality provided,” and Mr. Spitzer knows the vision is walled against loss. Witnessing does not unseal her. It only refuses to break her open by force. The chapter holds the ambiguity without resolving it: his silence is compassion, and it is also a leaving-be of a locked door, and the book will not tell us which weighs more. The Witness attends. It does not save.

His own self will not hold still either. Strangers take him for his dead brother; there are, the chapter suggests, two Mr. Spitzers, one dead and one alive, and he cannot always say which he is. Not One Self deepens in him from the dream-doubling of the wedding into a waking uncertainty about his own edges. He is becoming the man who cannot find the border between himself and the dead.

Catherine’s hunt for the “black coachman” is the sealed world’s search for its own certainty, one fixed point inside the dream she can locate and hold. Mr. Spitzer cannot confirm the coachman exists, and his inability is the difference between them: she needs one thing nailed down, and he has learned to live in the “beautiful tumult of undying confusions” without nailing anything. Her certainty-hunger is the sealed invention’s last demand; his tolerance of confusion is the open construction beginning to be possible.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that makes Mr. Spitzer’s silence a simple virtue, kindness with no cost, and the reading that makes it a simple failure, enablement with no love. It refuses to resolve the ambiguity of witnessing a sealed dream.

The footing is that the Witness stays with the painful, sealed thing without forcing it open and without sealing itself in turn, and the book gives that stance to Mr. Spitzer here for the first time in full. His plural self, his tolerance of “undying confusions,” his refusal to nail down the coachman, are the open construction taking shape in him against Catherine’s sealed one. Witnessing attends without fixing, and it is not the same as endorsing. The chapter will not weigh his silence as kindness or complicity, and the refusal to weigh it is the honest result.

For Reflection

When someone is sealed inside a comforting illusion, is it kinder to witness it or to break it open?

Is there a difference between staying with another’s sealed world and helping to keep it sealed?

What one fixed point does one keep hunting, the way Catherine hunts the coachman, in order not to face the confusion around it?

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

The Questions

Miss MacIntosh tears down the Columbus myth yet calls marriage a natural order and dreams lies. Why can she see everyone’s construction but her own?

Is Vera’s dream-life the truth Miss MacIntosh’s plainness lacks, or just the opposite seal?

When Vera wonders whether she killed Miss MacIntosh “by opening her eyes,” what is guilt doing to memory?

Miss MacIntosh is sharper here than her plainness first suggested, and the sharpness cuts unevenly. She debunks the Columbus story, she questions sacred narratives “derived from positions of authority,” she says a preacher is no necessity and worships outdoors. Toward other people’s inventions she keeps the construction open, seeing the received myth as a made thing that can be doubted. This is real, and it is to her credit.

But toward her own creed she seals the door. Marriage she presents as a natural order, like the mating of animals, not a built arrangement but a given; dreams and imagination she calls lies; her domestic training and her “rainy day” thrift she offers Vera as simply the way things are. The woman who will not let Columbus stand unquestioned will not question the frame she lives by. She can see everyone’s construction but her own, and that blind spot is the exact shape of the finished blueprint: open toward the far myth, sealed toward the near one.

Against her the chapter sets Vera’s inner life, the dreams and the imagined romantic future. It is tempting to make Vera’s dream-world the truth Miss MacIntosh’s plainness lacks. The chapter resists that too. Vera’s dream is not yet the open construction; it is the other pole, an inner sealed room answering the outer one, romance and adventure imagined as fixed as the domestic order it rejects. The book is not choosing dream over plainness. It is showing two seals facing each other.

Grief and guilt work on Vera’s memory throughout. She wonders whether she caused Miss MacIntosh’s death merely “by opening her eyes,” whether it was murder or “the key turning of itself in the lock.” The question cannot be answered, and the chapter does not answer it. Guilt has made her memory unreliable, folding the past into a present she cannot get clear of, and the unanswerable question is left standing, which is the honest thing to do with it.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes Miss MacIntosh’s practical creed for its wisdom, and the equal and opposite reading that takes Vera’s dream-life for the truth it lacks. Both are seals. It refuses, too, the settling of Vera’s guilt into either verdict, murder or accident.

The footing is the precise diagnosis of Miss MacIntosh: open toward the far construction, sealed toward the near. That is how the finished blueprint usually works in a person, not total blindness but selective sight, doubting the myths that cost nothing to doubt and enshrining the frame one lives inside. Vera’s answering dream is no freer. The stance the book trusts is the one neither of them holds, to keep even the near construction open, especially the one you live by. The frame you inhabit is built too, and hardest to see. The death stays unjudged, and the chapter lets it.

For Reflection

Whose constructions are easy to see through, and why is one’s own frame the hardest?

When a fixed dream answers a fixed duty, is either of them open?

What unanswerable question from one’s own past does guilt keep folding into the present?

The inventory of Miss MacIntosh’s things, wig, false teeth, corset, borrowed hats, lays out the parts of her plainness. If the plain self was assembled from props, what was it?

A “Christian woman with an honest mind” keeps a gambling deck with the “deuce of clubs,” the omen of death, turned up. What holds those “double motions” in one person?

The chapter itemizes the construction. Where the unsealing lifted the surface and the masks were named, this one lays out the parts: the wig, the false teeth, the corset, the mismatched borrowed clothing, the baseball cap and whistle and oilskin hat, the black umbrella carried indoors “like a shield.” The plain self was assembled. Every prop that made Miss MacIntosh look like unadorned bedrock is here on the table, and seen together they show that the plainness was Reality Is Constructed all along, a built surface as carefully kept as any of Catherine’s dreams, only built to look like no construction at all.

And the plurality is in the objects too. A “Christian woman with an honest mind” who calls gambling “the crafty Devil’s handiwork” keeps a deck of cards with the “deuce of clubs,” the omen of death, turned up. The chapter names these “dualities in one heart, these double motions,” and refuses to reconcile them. She is not a hypocrite to be exposed; she is a crowd, like everyone in the book, holding the honest woman and the gambler, the believer and the fatalist, in one unsorted self.

The room is The Past Doesn't Go Away made into a place. Crumbling cherubim, broken acanthus leaves, a broken ship’s compass, a torn almanac, cracked walls, everything decaying, everything the sediment of a past that will not stay behind. Miss MacIntosh tries to hold it off, cheese-cloth draped over the crumbling heads, the Bible chained to the table, small orders imposed on a general ruin. The imposing does not work, and the failure is the point: the past keeps rising, the decay keeps winning, and no chained Bible stops it.

The worn, patched, useful things are the chapter’s finest ambiguity. Saved for a “rainy day,” mended and re-mended, they are genuinely The Sacred Is Here, the resourceful tending of a plain life. And they are also the stage-dressing of the built plainness. The chapter will not let the reader choose. The umbrella is a real umbrella and a shield and a prop, all at once, and Miss MacIntosh is a real plain woman and a construction of plainness, both held open.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that turns the inventory into an exposure, Miss MacIntosh unmasked as a fraud in wig and false teeth, and the reading that takes her worn useful things as pure unbuilt virtue. Neither the caught-out hypocrite nor the saint survives the chapter.

The footing is that the plainness was assembled, a construction built to look like none, which is Reality Is Constructed at its most disguised; the contradictions in her are the plural self, not hypocrisy; and the decaying room is the past refusing to stay behind, unstoppable by any small imposed order. The worn objects are ordinary virtue and stage-dressing at once, and the chapter holds both. Even the plainest self is assembled, and the plurality and the decay are real. The chapter itemizes without concluding, and leaves Miss MacIntosh both plain woman and built plainness, unreconciled.

For Reflection

If one laid out on a table every prop that makes one look like oneself, what would be left over as the self?

What “double motions” does one hold that a closer look would refuse to reconcile?

Which of one’s plain, useful, virtuous things are also, honestly, stage-dressing?

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Pillars: Not One Self

The Questions

“If his brother had died, Mr. Spitzer would have lived.” Why can he not be sure which of them is the one who died?

He had “mapped out his entire life” and would not have “deviated by one inch from his course.” Is the planned life he lost something to mourn, or something he was spared?

He wonders whether there is “a non-aural music, a non-visual language, a reality not dependent upon the ear, the eye.” What reality would that be?

He collects stamps from “kingdoms this world had never seen, republics never marked upon any map.” What is he cataloguing?

The chapter opens on the undecidable death. “If his brother had died, Mr. Spitzer would have lived,” and the conditional is the trouble: he cannot be sure the condition holds, cannot be sure it was his brother and not himself who died on that great fall. Not One Self reaches the point where a man cannot say which of his two selves is the corpse. This is not confusion to be cleared up but the deepest form of the doubling the book has tracked in him: the border between the living and the dead brother runs through Mr. Spitzer so completely that he must reason about his own survival as a conditional, uncertain which side of it he is on.

Against the life he has, the chapter sets the life he planned and lost. He had “mapped out his entire life” and “would not have deviated by one inch from his course unless it had been planned,” a future of quiet musical study and undisturbed collecting, fame waiting patiently at his door. It reads at first as a loss, the orderly existence his brother’s death tore up. But the map is a finished blueprint, a life sealed in advance, deviating by not one inch, and by the book’s own terms it is the sealed thing. His brother’s death did not only rob him of the planned life. It broke the plan open, threw him off the mapped course into the unmapped, unsealed existence he actually leads. What he lost was a seal.

And the chapter reaches, in passing, toward the book’s next move. Mr. Spitzer wonders “if there was such a thing as a non-aural music, a non-visual language, a reality not dependent upon the ear, the eye.” He is feeling for a meaning that does not need its physical medium, a music without sound, a language without sight, and the wondering plants what the silent music will soon make real. It is the question of whether the sacred, the meaningful, the communicated, lives in the medium or beneath it, and Mr. Spitzer, losing the reliable evidence of his senses, is beginning to suspect it lives beneath.

His collections carry the same reach past the mapped and the given. He gathers “stamps from kingdoms this world had never seen, republics never marked upon any map,” cataloguing places that do not exist on any chart, the unmapped answering the unmapped life. The man whose planned map was broken now collects the mapless, the postage of nowhere, as though the loss of his sealed course had turned him toward everything that no course could contain. The unfinished life and the unmapped kingdoms and the medium-less music are one reaching: toward a reality not fixed by plan, sense, or chart, held open past every seal.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes Mr. Spitzer’s lost planned life for a pure bereavement, the orderly existence he should have had, and the reading that takes his uncertainty about which brother died for a mere muddle. Neither the stolen order nor the muddle is what the chapter shows.

The footing is that the border between the living and the dead brother runs through him so completely that his own survival is a conditional he cannot settle; that the life he mapped and lost was a finished blueprint, sealed in advance, so his brother’s death broke a seal rather than only stealing an order; and that his wondering after a non-aural music, a reality beneath the ear and eye, reaches toward the meaning that lives under its medium, which the silent music will make real. The lost plan was a seal, and the unmapped life is the open one. Mr. Spitzer collects the postage of kingdoms no map holds, and the chapter leaves him reaching past every chart.

For Reflection

Is the carefully planned life one has lost always a bereavement, or sometimes a seal one was spared?

Is there a meaning that lives beneath its medium, a music without sound, a language without sight?

What draws a person, after the loss of a fixed plan, toward everything no plan could contain?

And the book, having shown that witnessing without unsealing may be complicity, now shows that forcing the seal open may be its own violence. Neither pole is clean. The mirror from the tomb is as much an assault as Mr. Spitzer’s silence was an abandonment.

Her directness, which the chapter admires, is also her blueprint. Cousin Hannah “always believed in being direct,” believed it the way Miss MacIntosh believed in facts and Catherine in her dreams, as a sealed conviction about how life must be met. Grief moves under her constant motion. She is nomadic, grief-shadowed, always in transit, and the transit is the tell. Cousin Hannah carries a grief she will not stop long enough to face, and her endless doing, the causes, the travels, the rescues, is partly a way of outrunning it. This is Grief Doesn't End refused in a new key: not walled like Catherine’s, not become-material like Mr. Spitzer’s, but outpaced, kept just behind her by never standing still. The woman who would force Catherine to look in the tomb-mirror cannot hold still in front of her own.

And Mr. Spitzer cannot finish her. He visits her house after she is dead, tries to write her epitaph, cannot settle on one, cannot even recall the date of her death; no one mourned her rightly. The unfinishable inscription is Unfinished Is Honest turned on the most decisive person in the book. Cousin Hannah, who believed in directness and certainty and the final answer, cannot be sealed into a final line. The woman of the finished blueprint gets no finished epitaph, and the failure to complete her is truer than any completed inscription would have been.

The chapter refuses the reading that takes Cousin Hannah’s directness as its answer, the healthy confronter of reality against Catherine’s evasion, and the reading that takes her attempt to rescue Catherine as simple heroism. Neither the healthy realist nor the rescuer is the all of her.

The footing is that Cousin Hannah is the anti-Witness, forcing the seal open where Mr. Spitzer refused to disturb it, and the book shows the forcing as its own violence, no cleaner than his silence was clean. Her directness is a sealed blueprint, a certainty she has stopped questioning, and her constant motion outruns a grief she will not face. And her unfinishable epitaph is Unfinished Is Honest claiming even the most decisive figure: the woman of the final answer cannot be sealed into a final line. Forcing a sealed person open is not kinder than leaving them sealed, and certainty about directness is its own construction. Neither Mr. Spitzer’s silence nor Cousin Hannah’s mirror is endorsed, and her epitaph stays unwritten.

For Reflection

Is forcing someone to face a hard truth kinder than leaving them their comfort, or only a different kind of harm?

What conviction about how life must be met has one stopped questioning, and carried into every room?

What grief does one outrun by never standing still?

Esther will not “tell the jury” her story, and cannot “explain by the calendar what had happened.” What can the law not hold?

She is threatened with a lawsuit over “something she could not prove.” What is a court doing with a mystery there is no evidence for?

The lawsuit is the finished blueprint trying to seal what will not be sealed. A court exists to reach a conclusion, to say definitely what occurred and who is liable, and it is loosed on a woman whose whole truth is that nothing about her can be definitely said. The “legal entanglements like ropes thrown around her feet” are the seal reaching for the unsealed, the demand for a provable account thrown around a life that offers “some old feather, some old rosebud… a baby’s foot, her absent-mindedness.” The law wants the case closed; Esther is a case that cannot close, and the collision between them is the book’s quarrel with finality staged in a courtroom.

And she loves her woe. “She loved her woe, but it was hers and hers alone,” and the line is the chapter’s heart. Esther does not want her grief resolved, healed, taken from her, or explained; she loves it, holds it as her own possession, guards it against the court that would drag it into evidence. This is Grief Doesn't End owned to the fullest: grief not endured as an affliction to be gotten past but cherished as the truest thing she has, hers and no one else’s, not for the jury, not for the calendar, not for cure. To love one’s woe is to refuse the project of getting over it, and Esther refuses it completely.

What she wants is to be “let alone outside the pale of law.” Outside the law’s framework is where Esther belongs, in the region the settled system cannot reach or fix, the open country beyond the reach of verdicts. The book has shown the law elsewhere as one more construction, erroneous and arbitrary; here it shows a life that simply exceeds it, that asks only to be left in its own unprovable, unfinished, cherished condition, outside the pale. Esther is not lawless in the sense of criminal; she is beyond the law in the sense of beyond the finished framework, a woe that will not be tried, a mystery that asks only to be let alone with itself.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes Esther’s evasion of the law for guilt she is hiding, and the reading that takes her love of her woe for mere wallowing, a refusal to heal that she ought to overcome. Neither the concealed guilt nor the failure to heal is what the chapter shows.

The footing is that Esther’s open, unprovable condition is exactly what the law’s framework cannot hold, a mystery with no evidence set against a machinery built to close cases; that the lawsuit is the seal reaching for the unsealed, finality thrown like ropes around a life that will not resolve into fact; that she loves her woe, cherishing her grief as her own truest possession rather than enduring it as an affliction to be gotten past; and that she asks only to be let alone outside the pale of law, in the open country beyond the reach of verdicts. The unfinished exceeds the framework, and the grief is cherished, not cured. Esther keeps her woe and asks to be left alone with it, and the chapter grants her the region outside the seal.

For Reflection

What in a life is real and true and yet cannot be proved to any court or explained by any calendar?

Is there a grief one loves and would not give up, hers and hers alone, not for cure or resolution?

What lies outside the framework that wants every case closed, and who is only asking to be left there?

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Miss MacIntosh

Pillars: Grief Doesn't End

The Questions

Cousin Hannah spent her life on “overwhelming suffrage battles,” and at the end calls them “as nothing.” What did the public certainty seal her against?

If “the greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home,” what war did Cousin Hannah avoid by fighting all the others?

Her ambition was “boundless.” Is boundless ambition openness, or a blueprint that never stops building the same wall?

Three figures now have sealed their worlds, dream, plainness, action. What do their seals have in common?

This is where Cousin Hannah’s blueprint collapses, and it collapses in her own mouth. The woman of boundless action, of “overwhelming suffrage battles” and the “fight for freedom from man,” says at her death that her great battles “had been as nothing,” that “the greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home.” The edifice of public certainty, the causes, the travels, the standards never dragged in the dust, is revealed to have been a wall. She built a life of leaving home in order not to fight the war that was at home, and only at the end can she see the wall for what it was.

So the figure the book offered as Catherine’s opposite turns out to be her double. Catherine sealed herself in a dream against loss; Cousin Hannah sealed herself in action against the inner, domestic, unwon battles she could not face. Both built a finished blueprint and moved in. The dream and the deed look like opposites, retreat against engagement, sleep against vigor, and they are the same move underneath: a construction sealed tight enough to keep out the thing that most needed facing. The chapter completes a pattern the book has been laying since Miss MacIntosh, three figures, three seals, dream and plainness and action, each built to look like the answer and each a wall.

Her boundless ambition was the sealing itself. The chapter is exact that the ambition causes panic, that the relentless pursuit came at the expense of personal connections. Boundlessness sounds like openness, a will that will not be confined, but Cousin Hannah’s was the opposite: one certainty extended without limit, the same wall built higher and wider forever, never revised because never stopped. To keep building endlessly is not to keep the construction open. It can be the most sealed thing of all, a blueprint so busy extending itself it never has to ask whether it was the right blueprint.

And the grief she outran catches her here. The constant motion of the last chapter stops at the deathbed, and the domestic wars she never fought are finally in front of her, unwinnable now, unfought. This is Grief Doesn't End arriving late, the reckoning she spent a life outpacing, and its lateness is the tragedy. The book does not mock her, and it does not redeem her with a peaceful death. It lets her see, at the end, the shape of what she sealed against, and lets that seeing be both her one moment of openness and too late to act on.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes Cousin Hannah’s life of action as its endorsed ideal, and the reading that takes her deathbed reversal as a simple lesson that home matters more than the world. Neither the vindicated activist nor the tidy moral holds.

The footing is that Cousin Hannah’s public certainty was a finished blueprint, a wall of action built to keep out the domestic, inner battles she could not face, so that the woman offered as Catherine’s opposite is her double, dream and deed the same sealing move. Boundless ambition is not openness but one certainty extended without limit, the most sealed thing of all. And the grief she outran arrives at the deathbed, her one moment of seeing, and too late. Action can seal as tightly as dream, and endless building is not the same as keeping open. Cousin Hannah’s late seeing changes nothing she can still do, and the chapter lets the recognition stand without redeeming it.

For Reflection

What war does one avoid by fighting all the others?

Is one’s own ambition open, or one certainty extended without limit, the same wall built higher forever?

What would it mean to face the domestic, inner battle now, rather than at the deathbed?

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Pillars: Not One Self · Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · The Past Doesn't Go Away

The Questions

Catherine “did not know how many selves there were which came and went.” What kind of self cannot count itself?

“The one which did not return would be the immortal one. The immortal one would be the lost.” Why is the deathless self the missing one?

She holds there is “no difference between life and death…a difference which could never be resolved.” Is that wisdom, or the sealed dream refusing the last distinction?

She is lost inside her own ear, crying “Let me out of my ear!” What has her invention become when she cannot get out of it?

Not One Self here is not a freedom but a vertigo. Catherine “did not know how many selves there were which came and went,” her spirit moving “outside of her…going by many ways upon many errands,” a crowd too large and too scattered for its own member to number. This is the plurality the book has affirmed all along, but felt from inside a woman who cannot hold it, and the chapter gives it a devastating turn: “the one which did not return would be the immortal one. The immortal one would be the lost.” The self that never comes back is the deathless one, which means the deathless one is exactly the one who is missing. Plurality and grief meet in a single figure: to be many is to have one of the many always gone.

Her refusal of the last distinction is the sealed dream at its widest. There is, she insists, “no difference between life and death…a difference which could never be resolved,” and it would be easy to hear the book’s own openness in the line. But Catherine does not hold the distinction open the way Mr. Spitzer holds the butterfly and the moth open; she dissolves it, so that nothing can be lost because nothing was ever alive as against dead. This is the seal disguised as acceptance. Where the Witness stays with the unresolved, Catherine abolishes the terms, and abolishing loss is not the same as bearing it.

And the chapter shows her trapped inside her own construction. She is lost for years “inside her ear,” that “great continent no one had ever completely known,” walking its stairways and colonnades and crying “Let me out of my ear! … Where is the door?” The invention that was a paradise in the early chapters has become a labyrinth she cannot escape. This is what the sealed dream turns into once it is truly sealed: not a refuge but a maze with the door mislaid, the builder shut inside the building with no way out. The seal that kept loss out keeps her in.

The line the chapter turns on is quiet: “She travelled, but she never moved.” All the journeys, the night trains through impossible Alps and Gobi deserts, the carriage through the sleeping house, are motion that goes nowhere, a sealed world elaborating itself without ever opening. The Past Doesn't Go Away runs through it, the house moving in the night, the dead loves arriving, the furniture rearranging, but none of it is change; it is the same sealed room furnished over and over. Catherine is the book’s picture of what endless invention comes to when it is never let open: travel without movement, a crowd that cannot count itself, and one self always, immortally, lost.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes Catherine’s dissolving of life and death for the book’s own openness, and the reading that takes her endless dream-travel for freedom. Neither the wise acceptance nor the liberated wandering is what the chapter shows.

The footing is that her plural self is a vertigo she cannot hold, and the immortal self among the many is precisely the lost one, so that plurality and grief are the same fact in her. Her refusal of the difference between life and death abolishes the terms rather than holding them open, which is the seal disguised as acceptance. And her invention has become a labyrinth she cannot escape, travel without movement, the builder shut inside the building. Dissolving loss is not bearing it, and a sealed dream is a maze, not a refuge. Catherine goes on travelling without moving, crying to be let out of her own ear, and the chapter leaves her there.

For Reflection

When the many selves cannot be counted, is that freedom or vertigo, and what decides which?

Is abolishing the difference between what is lost and what is kept the same as learning to bear loss?

What construction of one’s own, built as a refuge, has become a maze with the door mislaid?

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Pillars: Not One Self · Unfinished Is Honest · The Sacred Is Here

The Questions

Is Mr. Spitzer a musician or a gambler, and can the book, or he, decide?

There is “a meaning of the music even when he had forgotten the score.” What survives when the notes are gone?

He is “always at one remove from that sad musician who was himself.” How is a man at a remove from himself?

If his musical life was a self-deception, “a lost musical career which should have taken place in a better world,” what is left of him?

The chapter will not decide which brother Mr. Spitzer is, and neither can he. He is a musician “if he was not mistaken,” and a gambler “on the other hand, if he was not a musician but had merely deceived himself.” The two selves, the composer and the gambler, the brother he was and the brother he buried, will not resolve into one answer, and the chapter holds the undecidability open rather than settling it. This is Not One Self at the end of its long development in him: not many selves he can survey, but two he cannot choose between, a man who genuinely does not know whether his life’s work is real or a self-deception, whether he is the artist or the gambler who dreamed an artist.

What survives the uncertainty is a meaning without its content. There is, the chapter says, “a meaning of the music even when he had forgotten the score,” even when he “had never known the arrangements of notes.” The music can be lost, the notes gone, the score forgotten, and still a meaning of it remains, a germinal music in the head that outlasts every particular of the piece. This is Unfinished Is Honest turned inward on art: what matters is not the finished, remembered, notated work but the meaning that persists when the work is gone, the sense of a music that survives the loss of the music. Mr. Spitzer may not have his score, may never have had it, and the meaning is there regardless.

He stands, the chapter says, “always at one remove from that sad musician who was himself.” Even his own identity as the musician is held at a distance, watched rather than inhabited, so that the self he might be is a figure he observes across a gap. This is the counterfeit self the book found earlier, the passing-for with no original, here grown gentle and habitual: Mr. Spitzer is not the musician but at one remove from him, beside the self he is, never quite occupying it. The remove is not a failure to be himself. It is what being a self has come to mean for him, a standing-beside rather than a standing-in.

And the chapter roots the undecidable question in the ordinary. Whether musician or gambler, Mr. Spitzer is among the mundane props of a life, the ace of clubs falling from his sleeve, the dice like his rattling bones, the horses’ hooves on the oval, the germinal music in his head that needs no concert. The meaning he keeps is not in a better world where the lost career should have taken place; it is here, in the falling card and the remembered-forgotten music and the elegiac mood of an ordinary afternoon. The Sacred Is Here holds even the undecidable self: whichever brother he is, the meaning of him is in here, the card and the dice and the music with no score, and not in the better world the career was supposed to belong to.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that wants Mr. Spitzer settled as either musician or gambler, the question answered, and the reading that takes his possible self-deception for a sad reduction, a man who was nothing he thought. Neither the settled identity nor the reduction is what the chapter shows.

The footing is that the two selves, musician and gambler, will not resolve, and the undecidability is Not One Self at the end of its course in him, held open rather than settled; that a meaning of the music survives the loss of the score, the germinal sense outlasting every note, so what matters is not the finished work but the meaning that persists without it; that Mr. Spitzer stands always at one remove from himself, beside the self he might be rather than in it; and that the meaning of him, whichever brother he is, is in the ordinary here, the falling card and the scoreless music, not in a better world. The self stays undecided, the meaning survives its content, and the sacred is in the ordinary afternoon. The chapter lets Mr. Spitzer be both brothers and neither, and asks for no better world to hold him.

For Reflection

Is there a question about who one really is that has no answer, and can be lived without one?

What meaning of a thing survives when the thing itself, the score, the notes, the content, is gone?

What would it be to live always at one remove from the self one might be, beside it rather than in it?

Characters: Madge Capehorn

Pillars: Not One Self · The Past Doesn't Go Away · The Sacred Is Here

The Questions

Madge feels herself “breaking into two.” Is that a breakdown, or the plural self arriving in someone who wanted to stay one?

Why does Madge meet her own pregnant, changing body with artifice and dread rather than with the ordinary?

The bus doubles back and Madge feels she has lived this before. What has happened to time?

What built things, “wife,” “mother,” “woman,” is Madge mistaking for fate?

Madge experiences Not One Self as terror. She is “breaking into two, herself and the other, this face unknown,” and the breaking frightens her because she wants to be one sealed thing. The pregnancy makes the plurality literal, two lives in one body, but Madge cannot receive it as the ordinary condition; she feels it as a self coming apart. Where the book elsewhere holds that the individual is the one illusion, Madge is the person that truth happens to against her will, and her dread measures how badly she wanted the sealed single self the book calls illusion.

This is why she refuses The Sacred Is Here of her own body. Her changing, growing, laboring body is the plainest ordinary fact there is, and she meets it with artifice and dread, wanting the smooth sealed surface rather than the open changing one. Her pregnancy she has called “this dark valley from which she might never return.” The ordinary miracle within her is exactly what she cannot hold.

Time layers around her. The bus doubles back, “phantom shapes which came and went,” and Madge feels she has lived this before, the past pressing into the present until sequence dissolves. The decay everywhere, broken gates, derelict windmills, is The Past Doesn't Go Away made scenery: nothing is behind her, everything accumulates in a present already going to ruin.

And she is caught inside built things she takes for fate. “Wife,” “mother,” the apparatus of what a woman is supposed to be, are agreements held in place by repetition, and Madge lives them as an iron circumstance she is a victim of. She cannot see the agreement as an agreement, and so she cannot revise it; the invention has sealed around her from the outside, which is its own kind of locked door.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that treats Madge’s fragmentation simply as trauma to be healed back into wholeness, as if the sealed single self were the health she should return to. And it refuses the reading that takes her dread of the body as mere private neurosis rather than a refusal of The Sacred Is Here the book keeps testing.

The footing is that the plural self is the ordinary condition, and Madge’s terror is what it looks like to meet that condition while still wanting to be one. The changing body is The Sacred Is Here at its most undeniable, and trading it for artifice is refusing the ground itself. The roles she takes for fate are built, and naming them as constructions is the first crack of daylight, even if Madge never finds it. She does not arrive at any of this; she rides on, breaking, and the chapter honors the breaking without curing it.

For Reflection

When the single self one wanted to be comes apart, is that loss or arrival?

What ordinary fact of one’s own body or life is met with dread instead of tending?

Which roles that feel like fate are actually agreements that could, in principle, be revised?

Characters: Esther Longtree

Pillars: Unfinished Is Honest

The Questions

Esther comes to think “successful conceptions had been her worst mistakes.” Why would the completed births be the failures?

She calls them “her unfulfilled abortions, her many births.” What is a birth that would have been truer left unfinished?

She wonders “why she wanted to give birth, to bring life into this sad” world. Is the wish to complete a thing always a good?

If the stillbirths are right and the live births are the grievous errors, what has happened to the meaning of success?

The chapter performs the book’s most startling inversion: the completed births are the mistakes. Brooding in the empty hours, Esther comes to think “that her past life had been different from what she had thought—that there had been mistakes of another kind, no miscarriages, successful conceptions, that these successful conceptions had been her worst mistakes, her most grievous.” The finished child, the delivered whole, the successful conception, is recast as the error, the grievous mistake, while the stillbirths, the unfinished, are quietly exonerated. This turns the ordinary reckoning on its head. What the world would call success, a live birth, a completed thing, Esther calls her worst mistake, and the book lets the inversion stand.

She names the completed births “her unfulfilled abortions, her many births,” and the paradox is exact. The birth that succeeded, that fulfilled itself in a living child, is the “unfulfilled” one, the mistake, while the abortion, the unfinished, the never-delivered, is by implication the fulfilled thing. This is Unfinished Is Honest pushed to its most radical claim: not merely that the unfinished is honest and the finished is dead, but that to complete, to deliver, to bring the whole thing into the world, can be the grievous error, and to leave it unfinished can be the truer, fuller act. Esther’s grief has arrived at a place where finishing is the sin.

This puts the very wish to complete under question. Esther wonders “why she wanted to give birth, to bring life into this sad” world at all, and the wondering is not idle. The desire to finish a thing, to deliver it, to bring the incomplete to completion, which every ordinary instinct treats as good, is here held up and doubted. Is it right to want to complete? Is the drive toward delivery, toward the finished whole, always to be trusted? The chapter does not answer with a flat no, but it opens the question the book has been circling from Esther’s side: the wish to seal a thing into completion may not be the innocent good it appears, and the impulse to finish may itself be the mistake.

So the meaning of success comes apart. If the stillbirths are exonerated and the live births are the worst mistakes, then success, in the ordinary sense of a thing completed and delivered, is no longer the good it was assumed to be. The book has praised the unfinished and dreaded the sealed all along; here, through Esther’s grief-sharpened brooding, it reverses the words themselves, so that the successful is the grievous and the unfulfilled is the fulfilled. This is not despair but the furthest reach of the open construction’s logic: a world in which completing a thing is the error and holding it open is the truth, where Esther’s everlasting, undelivered pregnancy is not her tragedy but her rightness, the one conception she has not spoiled by finishing it.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes Esther’s guilt over her live children for simple maternal pathology, and the reading that keeps the ordinary scale intact, in which a completed birth is a success and a stillbirth a loss. Neither the pathology nor the ordinary scale survives the chapter’s inversion.

The footing is that the completed births are recast as the grievous mistakes and the stillbirths quietly exonerated, so that the successful conception is the error and the unfinished is the truer thing; that to complete, deliver, and finish can itself be the sin, Unfinished Is Honest pushed to its most radical claim; that the very wish to finish a thing is put under question rather than trusted as an innocent good; and that the meaning of success comes apart, the finished no longer the good it was assumed to be. Finishing can be the mistake, and holding open can be the rightness. Esther’s undelivered pregnancy is the one conception she has not spoiled by completing, and the chapter lets that stand as truth rather than affliction.

For Reflection

Is there something one completed, delivered, finished, that might have been truer left open?

Is the wish to bring a thing to completion always a good, or can the impulse to finish itself be the error?

What happens to the meaning of success once the finished thing is no longer assumed to be the achievement?

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Pillars: Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · The Margins Reveal the Truth

The Questions

Mr. Spitzer’s failing eyes cannot keep “the difference between red and white.” When the senses go, what happens to the distinctions they drew?

He keeps “mistaking a beggar for a king or a king for a beggar.” If the eye cannot tell them apart, what held them apart?

He has “learned to be tactfully cautious, not offering his charities until he knew” who stood before him. What is that caution, when he can never quite know?

Why does the book give its clearest sight to a man whose eyes are dimming?

The chapter lets the categories dissolve as the senses fail. Mr. Spitzer’s “eyesight had grown dim,” his eyes “covered by a whirling fog,” and he can “scarcely knew the difference between red and white,” the red rose of the sun from the white rose of the moon. The failing of sight is not only a loss; it is a revelation. The distinctions the eye drew so confidently, red from white, this from that, turn out to have depended on the eye, and when the eye clouds, they come loose. What looked like differences in the world were partly differences the seeing supplied, and a dimming eye is one that stops supplying them, and so sees, in its way, how made they were.

The beggar and the king are the chapter’s sharpest case. Mr. Spitzer keeps “mistaking a beggar for a king or a king for a beggar,” taking the swallow-tailed gentleman for a poker-playing derelict and the derelict for a lord. The social grammar that sorts people into high and low, the categories that seem written into the world, will not hold for a man whose sight has clouded, because they were never written into the world; they were laid over it, a construction of rank the clear eye enforced and the dim eye lets slip. From the fog, the king and the beggar look the same, which is to say they were always, under the costume, the same, and only the sorting eye kept them apart.

His caution is the Witness’s answer to a world he cannot sort. Mr. Spitzer has “learned to be tactfully cautious, not offering his charities until he knew who the starving or sleeping” man was, and yet he can never quite know, so the caution is permanent, a way of moving among people whose rank he cannot read. This is not the caution of suspicion but of respect for an uncertainty he will not force. He will not pin the beggar or the king to a fixed identity his eyes cannot confirm; he stays provisional, tactful, holding the question of who stands before him open, which is the same provisional living he practices with the two chairs and the shifting relationships he refuses to codify.

And the chapter hands its clearest sight to the dimming eye. The Margins Reveal the Truth has been the book’s claim that those who do not fit the categories see the categories best; here it is the man whose sight is failing who sees, better than any clear eye, that the categories are made. His fog is a kind of vision. Where a sharp eye enforces the difference between king and beggar and never notices it is enforcing anything, Mr. Spitzer’s clouded eye lets the difference go and, in losing it, sees it for the construction it was. He is going blind into the truth that the clear-sighted are too clear-sighted to see.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes Mr. Spitzer’s failing sight for simple decline, a sad dimming, and the reading that takes his confusion of beggar and king for mere error, a mistake to be corrected. Neither the pathos nor the correctable error is what the chapter shows.

The footing is that the distinctions the senses drew depended on the senses, so a dimming eye lets them come loose and reveals how made they were; that the beggar and the king, the grammar of rank, were laid over the world rather than written into it, and look the same from the fog because under the costume they always were; and that Mr. Spitzer’s permanent caution is the Witness’s way of moving among people whose rank he will not force, holding open the question of who stands before him. The failing eye sees the categories are made, which the clear eye is too clear to see. Mr. Spitzer goes dim into that sight, and the chapter treats the fog as a kind of vision.

For Reflection

How many of the differences one sees so clearly are supplied by the seeing rather than found in the world?

If a clouded eye cannot tell the king from the beggar, what was keeping them apart?

Is there a sight that comes only when the ordinary, confident kind begins to fail?

Characters: Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Pillars: Grief Doesn't End · Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The Questions

Vera wants to “protect her from the knowledge of herself.” Is that the Witness’s compassion, or Mr. Spitzer’s refusal to disturb the dreamer, worn now by Vera?

Faced with the baldness and the missing breast, Vera reaches for ironing and the Hebrew calendar. What is the routine for?

Is Miss MacIntosh’s stripped body a barren “mystery no one can solve,” or the plainest mortal fact there is?

What does Vera owe the vulnerable person she can no longer un-see?

This is where Vera’s long apprenticeship to the Witness arrives. She has moved from the embryonic pity of the dream-wedding, through the horror of the unsealing and the dawning charity that followed it, to this: faced with Miss MacIntosh’s baldness and her missing breast, the body stripped to its mortal vulnerability, Vera turns to compassion. She wants to “protect her from the knowledge of herself,” to remember her even when forgotten. She stays with the exposed, deteriorating person and attends to her rather than recoiling. The Witness has come fully into her.

And the chapter is honest that it comes mixed. Vera also reaches for the ordinary as a shield, the wish to return to “the commonplace where nothing should be deranged,” the ironing of shirts, the learning of Hebrew measures and the Jewish calendar, routine pulled over the disturbing sight like a cloth over the crumbling cherubim. This is the idealized ordinary again, the plain used as cover rather than tended as ground, and it marks the flinch inside Vera’s compassion. Witnessing is hard, and she does it with one hand while the other reaches for something to not-see by.

The deepest ambiguity is in the protection itself. Vera wants to shield Miss MacIntosh from the knowledge of her own baldness, to let her keep her self-image intact. This is tender. It is also exactly what Mr. Spitzer did for Catherine, refusing to disturb the dreamer, keeping the sealed construction sealed out of love. Vera has learned the Witness and inherited its problem in the same motion: to witness a sealed person compassionately may be to help keep them sealed. The book sets her beside Mr. Spitzer without telling us whether either of them is right.

Under it is the plainest fact the book has reached. The baldness and the missing breast are called a “mystery no one can solve,” a barren, impoverished landscape, and Vera reaches for God, asking whether God too is bald. But the mystery is also simply mortality, the “dead tree of life,” the body’s deterioration that no housekeeping holds off. This is Grief Doesn't End at the body itself, the stripped mortal fact of a person one loved as solid, and Vera meets it with grief and compassion and the flinch toward routine, all at once, none of them resolved.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that makes Vera’s protection a pure and settled virtue, compassion with no shadow, and the reading that makes her retreat into routine a simple failure of nerve. Both flatten what the chapter holds open.

The footing is that the Witness arrives fully in Vera here, the stance the book has been teaching her since the dream-wedding, and it arrives mixed, with a flinch toward the idealized ordinary as cover. Her wish to protect Miss MacIntosh from the knowledge of herself is tender and is also the same ambiguous act as Mr. Spitzer’s refusal to disturb Catherine: to witness the sealed compassionately can be to keep them sealed. The stripped body is mortality plainly, held in Grief Doesn't End. Vera has learned to witness, and witnessing the sealed carries a real ambiguity the book will not resolve. Vera protects, flinches, grieves, and reaches for God, and the chapter closes without deciding whether her protection is kindness or one more locked door.

For Reflection

Is protecting someone from a hard truth about themselves compassion, or the keeping of their door locked?

What routine has one pulled over a sight one could not bear to keep looking at?

What does one owe a person one can no longer un-see as vulnerable?

Chapter 18

Other versions: Chapter hub · Research notes · The Wheel and the Spokes

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Pillars: Grief Doesn't End · Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act · Language Shapes What's Possible

The Questions

If meaning is “always moving toward something else, the something which cannot be put into our paltry language,” what can language actually hold?

Miss MacIntosh’s baldness is her stripped surface. Is what shows underneath a truth, or just another mask?

Vera calls her recoil “cruelty” and turns to charity. What has changed in her since the horror of the night before?

If “each must wear a mask which screens him from himself,” is there a face under the masks, or masks all the way down?

The chapter presses on the limit of language. Meaning is “always moving toward something else, the something which cannot be put into our paltry language.” Language builds the world, as the book has shown, and here it meets its edge: the built grammar cannot catch the thing that keeps moving past it. This is not a retreat from Language Shapes What's Possible but its honest completion. If words make worlds, they also fail at the seam where the world exceeds them, and Miss MacIntosh’s flat pronouncements, “Nothing that you think is true is true. Nothing that you see is real,” are that failure spoken from inside.

The masks are the chapter’s image for the plural self. “Each must wear a mask which screens him from himself,” and behind the mask is not a single true face but “the forever fading image of the other self, the lost soul,” the secret man in a woman and the woman secret and recessive in a man. There is no bare face waiting under the last mask. The self is masked all the way down, plural, receding, never resolving into one. Miss MacIntosh’s baldness, the stripped surface of the night before, does not reveal the real her underneath; it reveals another layer, another vulnerability, one more thing that will not be the final thing.

And Vera changes. The night before she met the unsealing with horror and violence; now she names that recoil “cruelty” and turns toward charity, “not only for their sakes but as a retribution for my cruelty to my darling.” This is the Witness advancing in her. She is learning to stay with Miss MacIntosh’s exposed vulnerability rather than recoil from it, to attend to the stripped and masked and plural person without needing her to be solid again. The pity that was embryonic at the dream-wedding is becoming a practice.

Under it all runs the “phantom of change,” the one thing that holds by never holding still, and the void it moves across. “How ephemeral are we! How transient were we.” This is Grief Doesn't End at the widest, grief not for one loss but for the transience of everything, held open rather than sealed against. The chapter does not resolve it into consolation. It stays with the ephemerality, and Vera’s new charity is what staying-with looks like when it turns toward another person.

What the Chapter Refuses, and the Footing It Offers

The chapter refuses the reading that takes the stripped Miss MacIntosh as finally revealed, the true face under the mask at last, and the reading that takes the limits of “paltry language” as a reason to stop speaking. Neither the final face nor the surrender of language is available.

The footing is that language builds and also fails at the seam where the world moves past it, and that failure is honest rather than defeating. The self is masked all the way down, plural and receding, with no bare true face waiting to be uncovered, not even under Miss MacIntosh’s baldness. And Vera’s turn from horror to charity is the Witness maturing, the stance that stays with the stripped and plural person without demanding she be solid. There is no final face under the masks, and the honest response to that is compassion, not recoil. The phantom of change keeps moving, the void stays open, and the chapter ends in Vera’s new tenderness rather than in any answer.

For Reflection

What in one’s own experience keeps moving past every word one finds for it?

If there is no final face under the masks, what is one actually looking for when one wants to know someone truly?

What recoil of one’s own might, looked at again, turn out to have been cruelty, and turn toward charity instead?
